lines.text: [music] Welcome one, welcome all — it's DVDASA, with your hosts David Choe and Asa Akira. Here we go.

We started a little late today. Me? Yeah, I think he was enjoying the song. We've got a super DJ fuck-fest today, and that's the beauty of the show — you never know what's gonna happen. Even we don't know what's gonna happen. So Bobby Lee and his brother Steve Lee just bounced, artist Esao Andrews just bounced,

and artist James Jean just closed his Skype window. And they say, in life, as one door closes, another one opens. So we were sitting here very somber — and then we have Nosaj Thing, in person, sitting here.

One of my favorite musicians is here. We got a graduate of the Choe method, Alvin Risk, up in this bitch right here. Sup. Yeah, boy. Whoop, whoop. And then, hailing all the way from the UK, stopping by in beautiful downtown LA — Feed Me. Hello, mate. What do you like to go by?

"Feed Me" is fine. Feed Me? So we've got Feed Me. And who are your lovely acquaintances right here? This is my beautiful friend Jake. What's up, Jake? How you doing, man? Hey. I also make music too. Oh yeah?
As Kill the Noise. Kill the Noise — and Feed Me. Yeah. Okay. And who's this handsome fellow right here? Jeremy. Hey, Jeremy. And you — you're the groupie? You're the groupie? He makes my clothes.
Oh, you're the product guy? Yeah. Oh, okay. You look like a product guy. You look like a product dude.
So, yeah — first of all, you guys are on tour right now, or what? I was. I did like five shows around the States for New Year's Eve. Okay. And I finished in California.
I did San Diego and LA. So, just to start — what do you mean, five shows for New Year's Eve? Yeah. Like, in one night? No. No, I did that last year, I think.
We did two in a night, which is exciting. You go on a plane. But this year, I just did five leading up, and then New Year's. Oh, so you're, like, super popular. No.
Well, maybe. It sounds like you are. I don't know anything about, like— He's very modest. Yeah, any time we, like— First of all, how old are you guys? Just to start off. 29. 28.
13. [everyone laughs] I knew I liked you. He looked the same 10 years ago. Yeah, I'm 37, and I listen to everything. First of all, I travel a lot. I do a lot of different jobs.
I'm with a lot of different people all the time. And every time I'm with a new group of people, they're always all into something. And I'm like, how did you even come across this?

When I was a kid, you listened to the radio and that's what you listened to — that was your access to whatever. And now, with iTunes and Pandora and whatever, like SoundCloud — the amount of, you know... it's like, okay, you got the new Kanye or Jay-Z album that everyone knows about, but then all these

millions of other bands and DJs — you know, it's so... I sound like an old fart when I'm like, you guys are all fucking huge DJs, and it's crazy, man. We all came out of the same kind of area. We were all

drum and bass, I guess, before — which was, like, underground UK music, right? So that's kind of my access to a lot of drugs, basically. Not actually — no, not until a few years ago. That was brief. So after the drum and bass — yeah, I was always quite a good boy. Well, I met

Alvin through Skrillex. Skrillex came by the place and he's like, "This is my friend Alvin, he makes music too." And he looks like Clark Kent — very mild-mannered guy in the background, not, you know, loud. Always wearing black. Be a good spy. Yeah. And I was like, oh, there's Alvin. Turns out Alvin is, like, the fucking

secret weapon — like a mega-monster. Whenever Alvin's here, he's like, "What is that?" and then he'll just remix everything while we're sitting there. Can you talk about any of the projects you're working on right now, or are those all top secret? Um, it's pretty much top secret.

Okay, so we'll talk about— all you guys always have cooler projects than my project. Yeah, these guys are geniuses. Money Mark's always working on— yeah, all the projects are always awesome. And I'm more excited to talk about the Choe method, because Alvin is one of the first graduates of the Choe method. He came here, um,
[removed]

he's coming all the time — he's coming all the time now. But he came a few months ago with Sonny and they showed me the top-secret videos and shit they're working on. Music that's, like, all amazing. Um, I did an album cover — yeah, Junk Food. Junk Food, amazing. Love all the songs on

there. And, um, I'm not scared to say how ignorant I am about this whole world. Like, DJs, for me growing up, was like Q-Bert, scratching, all that shit. And then it's a whole— when you show me concert footage of the shit you do now, it looks like

the Paradise City video — like, a hundred thousand people, concert venues, people going insane. But there's no guitar player, it's just you standing there going fucking nuts, and the people in the audience look like they're going fucking crazy, you know? Yeah, it's a party. Wait — like, what happens in a situation like— do you watch the stage

at a show like that? Yeah, I mean, it doesn't really feel real because there's so many people. No, no — I mean, when you go to a DJ's concert, do you watch the DJ, or is it like a party? Yeah, that's kind of how it's changed. People used to— that kind of frustrates me sometimes, because—

in the industry, we work harder and harder to make yourself the spectacle. But I think sometimes it's nice when people just dance with each other, right? They're kind of ignoring— just provide the music. But do you remember your first show, when there's, like, two people there? Yeah. Actually, my first show was at quite a big, unidentified London club. I'd never DJ'd in my life — I got forced into it by my

record boss. So I just kind of walked in — I didn't really feel like I had a right to be there. So you sort of fell into it? Yeah, I— well, yeah, I got bullied into it by a South London gangster. Oh, so it's interesting — gangs pushed you into music? Oh, well, no — yeah, he was like that,

that guy wasn't really a gangster. No, he's a bit of a plastic one. He's a fucking— he was a wanker. He'd camp outside my house— he actually still owes probably all of us money. That's the same guy we're talking about — Clayton. Yeah, yeah. He's definitely gonna watch this stuff.

Oh, man. Excellent. So then it is a fucking huge party. It's a giant party. Definitely. It's a huge party. I mean, what is the level of pussy at these things? Like, at the end of the show — it's like a rave, right? Or— That's an ADP. That's serious ADP. Like a legal rave.

It's like a legal rave now. Yeah, I mean— the drugs aren't as strong as they used to be. Not anymore, man. Think about it — we've all done Coachella and Lollapalooza and all that shit. That's not a rave. Yeah, those aren't raves. That's a fucking concert.
Do they still have, like, illegal raves now? Yeah, but we don't go to those things. Okay, that's, like, beneath you. Not beneath me. That's an after-party. It's not my kind of party.
Yeah, I don't know. So, going back to the important question — the level of pussy at the end of these things. The important shit. Yeah, I'm glad we defined whether it was a rave or not. [sarcastic]
Oh my God, DJs get so much pussy. Are you kidding? Yeah. The problem is, it's all, like, 16-year-old girls, though. So what's the problem? [everyone laughs]
[removed]

I frequently get electric shocks from my own equipment because of that. And then— you do, like, a two-hour, three-hour, five-hour, six-hour set? How long are your sets? Nah, two. I do, like, a live show, which is different.
Okay. So we have, like— I have, like, a 30-foot light sculpture that I built, and I control it. With the music? Yeah. It's a whole performance thing. It's an audio-visual thing.
Awesome. But, like, do you really have to be there? Yeah. That was the point — we made it so if I leave, it stops. That was part of the point. And is that every DJ?
No. No, come on — you've definitely heard that not many DJs do much. No, I really don't know anything. Like, I've been listening to the same music since high school. No, it changed totally, though.

Like, when I was a kid, it was the same thing — Q-Bert and whatever, people scratching. It was an interactive art form. Right. But I always kind of looked at it from afar, and I was a musician in my own head.

So DJing, to me, was kind of supplementary to that. So you're like, I'm going to be the guy that's like, I need to be here — I'm going to control these lights with the music, do a whole audio-visual presentation.

Exactly. Yeah. Otherwise, what's the point of me if I can turn it off? Like, it's an experience. Yeah, I get it. Well, you could easily just program it to do that, and have really exaggerated hand gestures, and make it look like— well, people do that too.

Those shows are more fun to stand behind the person and watch than to see from the crowd. I mean, it's mime — which actually says a lot more about the person, I think. But the bottom line is, you're pretending — they're fucking right there—

And the truth in both of those things is— like grinding over the decks without touching them. Right — and the truth in both of those things is: no one cares. Right? This is something we talk about a lot.

When you're jerking off, you'll take hardcore porn or softcore porn. If you're going to see a concert, of course you'd want the music to be live. And you care — you want to prove that you're doing something.

But if you decided not to do that, the same amount of people would show up. I'm not really, like, a natural crowd person, so I like to be busy with something. If I stand there just behind a booth, I start thinking, why the fuck am I standing here? Why are these people

looking at me? So if I've got something to do, then I feel like I have a purpose. And I think that's probably the mantra of life, isn't it? That's what we're all trying to do. Yeah, we're all trying to find a purpose. So you have, like, these existential questions going through your head while you're—

We are extremely existential, these two guys. You guys should learn the Choe method — it'll help you. I was actually quite interested. I was gonna ask Alvin, like — how has it affected your music? So what is it? I haven't really made much. Yeah, we're talking about it. Like, everyone should have— I wouldn't mind, like, it—
[removed]
So the fans will show up. Even when people are like, "Did you know Beyoncé was lip-syncing?" — nobody cares, they still come to see her, right? So— although I will say—

Yeah, I would watch that. Wow, that was amazing. I would pay to go see that. But you know what, Mark? That was so awesome. It doesn't bother me if a singer lip-syncs. Like, when Mariah lip-syncs, because she's dancing like crazy— No, Mariah doesn't. But it doesn't matter. Beyoncé — yeah, like, if they're dancing or whatever.
But I think when a rapper lip-syncs, I'm like, that's horrible — it would make me think less of them. Rappers don't lip-sync, do they? I don't know. Which rappers lip-sync?
But if they did— I want to fucking whack their asses. But do you know what I mean? That's faking it, and that would make me think lesser of them. Right, I'm sure there's rappers that do that.

Well, that just strikes me as— as long as you can remember the words, you don't really need to warm up, you're just kind of rapping. So if it's that easy, then maybe you should save someone else the trouble.

Yeah. So then what's the come-down after a show like that? You do two hours, you're fucking working the lights, the music, you're pouring sweat, you walk off stage — do you, like, go to your room and go to sleep? Do you go out hunting 16-year-olds instantly? Do you really?
[removed]
Poon, what is going on there, man? That was nice. Do you follow DJs and all that stuff, Poon? No. No? All right, go back to sleep. What's up with the dance, and all the kids dancing?

There's no dance. Yeah, there is — that's what confuses me. What is the dance now? The dance now is jumping up and down, isn't it? Straight up and down. It used to be, like— there was the shuffle in LA, and then, yeah, I don't know. I guess different places do different stuff. What do you mean, the dance?

Like the electric slide? No, like— seriously, for New York hardcore, kind of punk music, there'd be, like, a couple of dances. Oh, like ska. Yeah. In Eastern Europe, there's, like, jump style. Okay, I see what you're saying. And the style for you guys is just jumping up and down.

Well, I don't know. I mean, anyone that actually wants to dance at one of the concerts kind of relegates themselves to the fringe, where there's a bit more space, right? Because we cram them in, so everyone in the middle has the option of standing still or jumping up and down — right — or punching each other.

Just beating the shit out of— okay, what about those guys who spin shit? Those guys who spin shit. Like glow sticks and stuff? Yeah, they're around, they're around. Especially, like— oh, gloving? Wait, shit gets aggressive at the shows?

There's a lot of punching and fighting and moshing? Gloving. Man, the biggest mosh pit I've ever seen was for Sonny. Like, I've been to— shit, we worked with Korn — we've been to a lot of metal shows.
The craziest mosh pit I've ever seen was Sonny in Europe. Does he stop the show and say, "Everyone stop fighting each other"? He has done that in the past, for sure. We all have.

I mean, that's not fun. People leave. Well, yeah — you guys are trying to promote a good time, and then there's people getting socked in the, you know— why do they do that? Sometimes they're nice, though.

Sometimes they're, like— if someone falls, I've seen them all kind of push each other back, pick them up, and he gets a pat on the back. In Brazil last year, some kid had an epileptic fit while he was in there, and I had to stop the music, and they stretched him out.

But then he was waving. What a shitty time to have an epileptic fit. How do people even know? Yeah, exactly. But that shows they have some semblance of— I'm like, whoa, that kid can dance. [everyone laughs]
Dave, you're a hug ambassador — you should go to some of these. Oh, yeah. You're both hug ambassadors. Yeah, you're a hug ambassador too. What are you talking about? Dave's a way better hugger.

No, you're— what are you talking about? You're the best hugger. Money Mark, going out, passing the torch over. He's going to go to a secret thing. No such thing. Yeah, secret project. Secret Money Mark.
That was a great performance. Oh, yeah. All right. Great to meet you guys. See you, man. Money Mark out. Nice one. No such. I'm picking up the baton. You're going to have Money Mark on it.
So take me through this a little bit, because I— I do my own version of, like, traveling and doing art, but it's always just me. It gets crazy sometimes, but, you know, whatever.

When I see you guys— you know, I know from Alvin and Sonny, the schedule just looks insane. City after city, party after party, fucking drugs, chicks — it just looks like fucking mayhem and chaos. How do you just— how do you function in that kind of environment?
How do you do anything? Well, he doesn't drink. That's a good one — that comes— what, anymore? What— I admire that about this guy, that he doesn't drink. That's a hard thing to do.

I love drinking. So you guys get wasted at that thing? Frequently. But then you've got the next show the next night. I just get up and do it again. Just do it. Well, British people are really good at that shit.

Yeah, British people are really good at drinking. British people get off their face, right? Wasted. And then it's just like, okay. Yeah, life goes on. Have a proper English breakfast, you know — fucking beans and toast.

Yeah, a hangover is a quarterly inconvenience for me. I'd rather just keep going. But to me, I worked my whole life to get to a position where I could tour like that, so when I got the opportunity, I wasn't going to do anything except keep going. I never thought, like,

"this is too much." The only thing I've done — last year I took a few months off because I literally ran out of time to do the things I liked, which was making music and drawing and stuff. So that's awesome. So you guys, like— you guys get off stage

and then have existential conversations? Nah, nah. I was just going to say — the first thing when you said that, I remembered when we were in Sweden with Flux, or one of those places, and we were putting candles in the leaf blower. Yeah, we'd stolen a leaf blower backstage,

blew candles out of it, and bananas, and then we used it to destroy our friend's dressing room, and then we carbon-monoxide-poisoned ourselves and staggered out. Oh my God, what assholes. So instead of fucking girls, we're just breaking shit. So— the shady guy that hasn't been talking, the t-shirt guy—
[removed]

You're going crazy. You're going crazy now. I like blowing up microwaves. That's probably my favorite thing to do. Blowing up microwaves? Glow sticks. You guys are like Bart Simpson. I got photos of his microwave antics — everything from glow sticks to fruit to other electronics.

They are raves. Those glow sticks — they're raves. And are you married? No, no way. So how do you maintain a relationship with this kind of— yeah, is your wife, like, super jealous? Do you take her with—

We all know each other from different places — from, like, real esoteric dance music. Like, real weird shit. And then we all met Sonny in different ways too. Who's this Sonny person? Skrillex. Oh, okay.
That's his name? Yeah. Sonny? Yeah. Interesting. What would you have called him? He looks like— I don't know — Matt or Brian? Like a Frank or something? Wouldn't be the same. Not a Sonny.
So what are you up to right now? What's the plan? Are you on break right now? I just got back from New Year's in Australia. I was actually with Jake. What did you guys do on New Year's?
We played at— I played on Bondi Beach. I don't know where you were. On New Year's Eve, I was in Perth. And then on New Year's Day, I was in Sydney. Yeah, we were in Sydney on New Year's Day.
Whoa, you guys live awesome lives. It's not bad. Are you on the ship? No, I'm not. Are you on the ship? I'm in the studio. I still want to do that. I did it last year, though. What's the ship?
Do they fly you first class? It sounds like a great place to— Do they fly you first class? Sometimes. We fly so much that we usually just get upgraded. What's the ship?
Holy Ship. It's a cruise. A rave. In Miami. And it stops at some islands. What happens if you take a rave to international waters? That's what it is. Do people jump off the boat and go crazy?
No. I'm surprised people haven't, but it hasn't happened. Knock on— wait, how long is it for? It's for, like, three days. And no one gets raped? I don't think that's happened to you.
[removed]
These people, for three days — that's most certainly happened. What is it? It's a cruise, and you've got, like— how many DJs on the boat? There's a lot, isn't there?

There's, like, 30 or something like that. It's massive. It's one of the biggest cruise ships in the world this year. It's super massive. And they have, like, Pharrell on there this year, on top of all the DJ stuff. There's some live performances on there as well. So you guys are all, like, DJs,

but do you guys just— when the music hits, do you just grab the mic and start rapping? Or singing? He loves a little sing-song. He sings. Do you have a good voice? Yeah, he does — he's got a great voice. He does. Sometimes I catch Alvin just dancing by himself. It's pretty cool.
Really? Yeah, I love it. It happens. Yeah. So, do you guys have anything you want to promote, or anything? Promote? Yeah. Not really. No — you guys are just fucking— what are you talking about?

You guys — out of all the people we've ever had on the show, I feel like you guys must have the most things to promote. Nah, they're already being promoted. They fucking are. But— fucking, the world, everywhere, they're selling out shit, there's millions of kids— they're like, "We have people for that. I'm just trying to have

a lovely time." Oh, okay, that's pretty cool. I didn't even expect to be here. No, we didn't expect to be here. This is a pleasure. Have you seen Jon's art? No, I have not. He's an amazing artist. Where do I see your art? On my laptop, if you want to look. I mean, do you have

like, art shows and stuff, or— no, I'm trying. He will. Yeah, I'll check it out, thank you. But besides your laptop, is there nowhere else I can see it, like online? Well, I mean, I do all my own album sleeves and covers and various other stuff — some animation work.

I'm involved in— I do the artistic direction for our show. What else do I draw? I don't know. You've got that animatronic. Oh, yeah, we spent the last— I forgot about that. We spent, yeah, my Feed Me mascot.
So we spent the last couple of years building an animatronic robot of it that we can use in a film, which I'm trying to budget at the moment. You did a figure or two, right?

Like a— yeah, the small one. Yeah, that's how I know these guys — that's what we're working on now. Yeah, sick. So, um, vinyl toys. I can't fucking— sorry, Jason's all the way in the back over here. You can play whatever you want, man. So you just got back from tour, right, Jason?
Uh, yeah, I was on tour for two months. What's— back now? So, okay — since I sound so stupid about all this shit — like, I love your stuff, but what is that considered, that type of music?

Uh, I don't know, my stuff is just more, like— it's not super high-energy party, it's just more downtempo. I know — so is that just— you're like, that's just electronic music? Yes. I toured with this guy.

Sadcore? Is it called sadcore? We could coin it now, I don't know. But, yeah — November, I was touring with this guy named James Blake, and December I had the craziest routing. I went to Tokyo and came back, went to Shanghai and came back, then went to Paris and came back. How are you holding it all together? No, I'm good.

I was tired, but now I'm cool. I'm back home for, like, this month, so — recording. So when you come back home, it's just right back to work? Yeah, yeah. You guys are crazy. So when you DJ, like, what time do you go to bed? Uh, it depends. Sometimes it's hard to— you can't— it's hard to fall asleep

right when you get— so are you one of those, like, wake-up-at-6-p.m.-type people? Uh, no. When I'm home, I try to maintain a normal schedule. When you're DJing— but when DJing, it's just hard. Is it, like, the stripper life, you know what I mean? I don't know, like — you have all this
adrenaline from the show. Like, you're asleep 9 to 5. Yeah, right. I don't know. You guys are talking to the wrong DJs, man. We're, like, the ones that are actually doing cool shit. Yeah, I mean—
Those guys fuck everybody and just get fucked up all the time. Yeah, I'll be honest with you — I'm like you, though. I'm in porn, but, like, I'm so fucking boring. Like, I'm in bed by 10.
Well, you're— right, you're probably good at what you do, then, right? Yeah, I mean, I'll be honest — I hate DJs. Like, most DJs, I think, are horrible, and I'm like, this is so shitty.

Yeah, you guys aren't douchey at all. Like, I fucking hate DJs. I never wanted to be a DJ — I was trying to make music. So the DJing was something I just got bullied into. I was like, ah, okay, I'll do it. And then it becomes, like, a lifestyle that you become attached to.

Right. But I don't really associate— the DJing is sort of how the music gets performed. Yeah, it's just a replacement for what used to be a rock concert. We all produce the music as well, you know, so that's really— I feel like what we're— yeah, if it had been 30 years earlier,

I would have been forced to play an instrument. We're producers, yeah — before DJs. You mentioned earlier, like, DJ Q-Bert and all those guys. Yeah, like, they're DJs, but I'm like, they're performing.

That's the shit that I grew up listening to. And I run a label with Craze, I'm buddies with A-Trak, all those guys. Right. That's where my inspiration to get involved in music came from — watching all those guys scratch.

Right, and all that kind of shit. And I remember, in that time, people calling them DJs, and I was like— and the turntable wasn't an instrument, you know what I mean? Right. Oh, it's definitely an instrument. Yeah, it's like — man, you guys aren't paying close enough attention to that. And then it became kind of my mission to be like, fuck you, this is like—

this is a fucking instrument, in the same way that— like when you see DJs up there, you're like, oh, those guys are just fucking— as Money Mark was doing, twisting the fucking knobs and shit — and it's like, yeah, we're twisting the knobs up there right now, but all of us spend an incredible amount

of time in the studio, away from our— well, you guys are DJs that make your own music. I'm talking about DJs that just play other people's music. And yeah, there's a whole thing to that also, but— you know, Dan the Automator, Money Mark, and Kid Koala were

here, we were all jamming, and Kid Koala was like, "Hey, I'm gonna bring my friend Jason." That's the first time I met Nosaj. Yeah, and he comes over — FYF Fest, by the way, man. Oh, sick. Yeah. And I'm like, oh great, we need another fucking DJ up in here — I'm like, Money Mark and Kid Koala are

already here. And then Jason brings— what's the machine that you like to use? Um, it's just a MIDI controller, it's called, like, the MPD32. And then that thing — he brings it out and proceeds to just fucking rip on it, like he's playing— I've never seen— I still, to this day,

I've never seen anyone play like that. I mean, he brings this thing out — MIDI, you know, like the keyboard — it's just, each button does everything, but he's literally playing it like it's a guitar, like he's fucking finger-banging this thing and hitting this button, twisting these knobs, and it's like he's making an original song, and I'm like, this is fucking insane,

you know? And he's like, "It's easy, Dave, you do it." And I'm like— no, I can't, I can't do it. So, I mean, that's like— oh, I'm like, whoa. It brought a new level of respect for me too, I was like, whoa, that's fucking crazy. I mean, you're pretty much the best of anyone I've ever seen. Yeah,

you are, you are — you're the best. And, um, thank you. So that's what I'm saying — you're saying you got pushed into it by some weird wanker drug-gangster guy— Pretty much sums it up. Yeah. For the rest of you guys, when was it where you're like, fuck, this is what I want to do

with my life? Like, what was the— Well, to me, when I first did my first DJ set, I had a few of my own tunes that I'd cut to vinyl records, and the CDJ had just come out, so I could play a CD I'd burnt at home. But the stuff wasn't finished. When I got to the point

where I could just play my own music, I felt like I was actually worth coming to see, because I was like, right, this is my show now. So then it was just a case of furthering that, trying to get out of what I was doing. I felt like the industry we were initially in was quite constricting.
It was run by, like, an old guard, it was a bit— glass ceiling, right. What kind of musician were you before? Musician? I played in an orchestra at school, and played guitar and piano and stuff.
Yeah, all the really good DJs that I like, or even have on the show — they all play an actual instrument also. Uh-huh. You know, which is cool. It helps. Yeah, it helps a lot.
It saves a lot of time later. Yeah. Interesting. So, you guys — any of the groups need a roadie? How much can you lift? I can lift a lot. My stuff was low. So what's up with you?
[removed]

I don't know, my schedule is changing right now because I'm thinking of holding on to a few things, quitting a few things, so that I have more free time. I'm trying to write a second-book draft. Really? Yeah. What's this one going to be? My goal is to have 60,000 words done by May.

I don't know how the fuck all you guys are so fucking disciplined and all this shit. Well, that's the thing — I've been so busy. No, but I talked to Asa about it when she was writing the book — she would wake up— Yeah, I wrote every morning. I don't have that anymore. You want me to wake you up at certain times?
I mean, that's sort of been your job for the last year, but— okay, you can start tomorrow doing that. Maybe not 1 o'clock in the afternoon. Oh, sorry, I was doing it. No, for myself, like, I don't—
Like, when Sonny and Alvin showed me their rough cut for their music video, I was like— I know a lot of it's in the editing, but I'm like, this looks like the most insane party ever.
Like, I would lose my fucking mind. I mean, you guys are a little bit older — none of you guys are, like, 21 or whatever — but I would fucking go crazy. I go crazy now.

I'm fucking 37. Like, I'll wake up tomorrow morning and be like, this painting right here hasn't been finished in a year. I started it a year ago. And every day I'll have the thought — today will be the day I finish that painting.
Like, I could sit here right now and start, you know. But it's also easier to have— okay, for example — you're publishing all your own shit, right? Yeah. So I'm sure it's much harder to motivate.

Like, for me, I have a deadline — or else I have to give the money they advanced me back. Right. Like, it's a little bit different. Creating tension within a self-employed environment is always a struggle.
Like, we have managers that you kind of have to ask, earlier, to hassle you. And then when it comes, you're annoyed at them. But you create the tension to make sure you had those deadlines.
